The factory closed on a Tuesday. No warning. No severance. Just a chain on the gate and a photocopied letter taped to the fence. Three hundred workers showed up that morning expecting a shift. They got a parking lot and silence instead. The mayor called it a tragedy. The company called it a restructuring. The workers called it something else entirely. Within a week, the ripple effects hit every business on Main Street. The diner lost half its lunch crowd. The hardware store cut its hours. The daycare center -- the only one in town -- started turning away families who could no longer pay. This is what happens when an entire community depends on a single employer. It is not a new story. But for the people living it, the pain is sharp and immediate. They do not care about economic theory. They care about rent.
